d.title: Three conditions, and what to do when each one breaks
d.caption: **The theorem makes the distribution of the *mean* normal — not the data — and it asks for three things, all of which fail in real work.** Knowing which one broke tells you what to do instead, which is the only reason to memorise the list. **Finite variance is the one that fails totally rather than gradually:** the mean of 10,000 Cauchy samples is distributed like a single Cauchy sample, so averaging buys you nothing at all. And the convergence rate is governed by skewness, so n > 25 times the squared skew is the usable rule before trusting a tail probability.

d.title: Three estimators of one variance, and the unbiased one loses
d.caption: **The three differ only in the denominator, and the unbiased choice is not the most accurate.** Dividing by n−1 is correct on average across samples; dividing by n+1 is biased further still and yet has the smallest mean squared error — the error you actually pay. **Unbiasedness is a constraint you may choose to impose, not the goal**, and imposing it costs accuracy here. That is the whole bias-variance trade in one table, and shrinkage is this trade used deliberately: pull an estimate towards a prior guess, lose a little bias, gain more variance back.
d.left: divide the sum of squares by

d.title: Four guarantees, all of them asymptotic
d.caption: **Every promise maximum likelihood makes is about what happens as n grows without bound**, which is exactly why the failure cases are all small-n or boundary cases. **Invariance is the one worth knowing:** the MLE of any function of a parameter is that function of the MLE, so the MLE of sigma is the square root of the MLE of sigma squared, immediately. Unbiased estimation offers nothing of the kind — the unbiased estimator of a variance does not square-root into an unbiased estimator of a standard deviation.

d.title: Precision is expensive, confidence is cheap, and variance reduction is free
d.caption: **This ordering surprises almost everyone.** Width is twice the critical value times sigma over the root of n, so **halving the width costs four times the data, every time** — while going from 95% to 99.9% confidence costs only 68% more width. The third lever is the one teams forget: **pairing or regressing out a pre-experiment covariate narrows the interval without collecting a single extra observation.** At a correlation of 0.8 pairing multiplies the effective sample size by five, and CUPED typically cuts variance by a third to a half, permanently.

d.title: Why the discrepancy is divided by what was expected
d.caption: **A gap of 10 is enormous where 12 were expected and invisible where 10,000 were** — dividing by the expected count is what makes those two comparable, and it is the whole design of the statistic. The output worth reporting is not the total: **the standardised residual per cell, anything beyond plus or minus 2, names the cell that drove the result**, which is the actionable part. And the approximation needs expected counts of roughly 5 or more; below that, use Fisher's exact test or a permutation instead of trusting the table.

d.title: Read the interaction first, or the main effects will lie to you
d.caption: **A main effect is an average over the other factor's levels, so if the factor did different things at different levels, that average is meaningless** — and an average of +10 and −10 is zero. A drug that helps one group and harms another shows no main effect at all while being extremely consequential. **Which fixes the reading order: interaction first, and only if it is absent do the main effects mean what they appear to mean.** Two separate one-way tests cannot find this, because neither design has a term for it.

d.title: Six defensible choices take a 5% false-positive rate to 23%
d.caption: **Nobody in this sequence is being dishonest, and that is the point.** Each step is an ordinary analytic decision — the data looked skewed, so a non-parametric test; those two points looked like outliers, so a standard 2-sigma rule — and each is made *after* seeing the data. Take the best p-value of the six on data with no effect at all and you are wrong nearly a quarter of the time. **Optional stopping is worse on its own, at 28%, and with unlimited patience it converges to 100%.** Pre-registration costs a document and eliminates the entire class.
d.left: choices made after seeing the data

d.title: Highly significant, and of no consequence whatsoever
d.caption: **Two million observations and a difference of 0.05 in a hundred: p = 0.0009, which any journal would call highly significant.** Now read the effect: Cohen's d of 0.0032, two distributions overlapping 99.87%, and a randomly chosen treatment case beating a randomly chosen control case 50.1% of the time instead of 50.0%. **The result is real, replicable and worth nothing** — significance and importance are independent, and a p-value cannot tell them apart. Which is why the comparison that matters is the interval against the smallest effect you would act on, not against zero.

d.title: At twenty tests a false positive is more likely than not
d.caption: **Alpha is a *per-test* error rate, so running many tests does not risk a false positive — it guarantees one.** Twenty tests at the 5% level give a 64% chance of at least one, and at a hundred tests it is essentially certain. **The expected-count form is the more useful one, because it does not saturate:** alpha times m says a 20,000-gene scan produces about 1,000 findings from noise alone, which “99.4%” does not convey. Correlation between tests softens this but never removes it — at rho = 0.95 across 20 tests the rate is still nearly four times nominal.

d.title: The tests nobody counted as tests
d.caption: **Explicit multiplicity is easy to see and easy to correct; this is the kind that does the damage**, because none of it is recorded as a test. Five binary splits give 31 subgroups, and hunting through them reaches a 34% false-positive rate on data with no effect. A 25-metric dashboard turns something green 72% of the time under the null. **And nobody corrects across experiments: a hundred experiments a year at the 5% level ships five noise features annually.** The one deliberate exception is the guardrail metric — correcting those makes you less likely to detect harm, which inverts their purpose.

d.title: Three bootstrap intervals, each correcting what the last one ignored
d.caption: **What separates them is bias and skew, and on skewed data the difference in actual coverage is several percentage points** — which is the only thing that matters about an interval. Start at the percentile method, add a location correction, then add corrections for median bias and for skew. **BCa is the modern default, and the reason to reach past the simple one is that the percentile interval is optimistic exactly when the estimator is biased** — the case you cannot see from inside the bootstrap. Verify coverage by simulation rather than trusting the nominal level.

items.label: Percentile
items.desc: take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the bootstrap values; simple, and optimistic whenever the estimator is biased

items.label: Basic
items.desc: reflect around the observed value to correct for location bias, which is why the quantiles come out reversed

items.label: BCa
items.desc: corrects median bias with z-zero and skew with an acceleration term from the jackknife; the modern default

items.label: Then check coverage
items.desc: simulate it rather than assuming the level; a 95% interval covering 89% of the time is the failure you cannot see

d.title: Sixty heads in a hundred: borderline significant, and the evidence favours the null
d.caption: **A two-sided binomial test gives roughly p = 0.057 — the classic “trend” — while the Bayes factor is 0.91, very slightly favouring fairness.** They disagree because they ask different questions. The p-value asks how surprising 60 heads would be if the coin were fair. The Bayes factor asks whether a model free to assume *any* bias predicted this data better than one that assumes none — **and a model free to put its mass anywhere pays for that freedom.** This is the Jeffreys-Lindley effect, and it is why a borderline p-value is weaker evidence than it feels. A Bayes factor below a third is the statement no frequentist test can make: evidence *for* the null.
